hook: The philosopher emperor who wrote notes to himself on how to live.

pages.x: Marcus was born in Rome in 121 to a rich family. Emperor Hadrian noticed him early and nicknamed him "Verissimus", "most truthful". At 12 he took up the plain life of a philosopher, wearing a rough cloak and sleeping on the ground, until his mother persuaded him to use a bed.
pages.cap: Hadrian, who picked him out as a boy

pages.x: Adopted by Emperor Antoninus Pius, he became emperor in 161, and at once shared power with his adopted brother, Lucius Verus. It was the first time Rome had two emperors at the same time.

His reign was full of trouble. Soldiers coming back from the East brought a plague, perhaps smallpox, that killed millions across the empire. Germanic tribes broke across the Danube, and Marcus spent most of his last years in army camps on the frontier.

At night in his tent he wrote notes to himself in Greek, never meant to be published, on how to live well: "You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realise this, and you will find strength." They survive as the Meditations, one of the best-loved books of philosophy.

In 172 a Roman army was trapped by Germanic warriors and dying of thirst. Suddenly a storm burst, giving the Romans rain to drink while lightning struck the enemy. Christians and pagans each said their own god had sent it. The scene is carved on his column in Rome.

pages.t: The end of a golden age
pages.x: He died in 180 on the Danube frontier, aged 58. His son Commodus, the villain of the film Gladiator, was a disaster, and historians mark the death of Marcus as the end of the golden age of Rome.

Marcus Aurelius was the last of the "Five Good Emperors", the philosopher king Plato dreamed of. His Meditations are read today by millions, from soldiers to athletes, as a guide to staying calm and doing one's duty.
